utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Joanna Korner and for the first time Mr. Timothy Resch, who as I've assured Mr. Ackerman is not working on this case but is here out of interest, and as usual, Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Ms. Korner. Good afternoon to you. "To you" means the plural. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. Sitting out in the public gallery is a new intern who is a third year law student from university of south Texas in Houston. I have talked with Ms. Korner and she would have no objection to him entering the courtroom and sitting at the backbench, if it's okay with Your Honours, but I didn't want to put him in here until I cleared it with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose he's the one without the jacket?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's him. It's up to you, Your Honours. And it's not an important issue but it would be nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay with you, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. No problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope he got the message too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he did. We really didn't plan on this until the last minute, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will be better from now on. Let me, before Ms. Korner gets to do it I want to eat in her words, humble pie, in mine, crow, about whether she asked for the reason or not. She didn't. And I'm glad I didn't bet money on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just while the witness is brought in, no reason to stop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I forgot I was reminded yesterday, to make the Colonel's workbook, whatever he call it, an exhibit at the end of the day. And appropriately perhaps could it be made P1600?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that will be it, P1600 and there is another thing that you promised us yesterday. You said that you were informed by Mr. Brdjanin that he would be making further reference to the war diary, and that you would have it photocopied and -- ah, here it is. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we might not also give it an exhibit number at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought it already had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought I did exhibit the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does have. It does have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be I suppose the new 1590 because what we had was as far as we are concerned we only had two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I mean, Your Honour, I think I exhibited the whole.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. Ackerman is going to use it we might as well have the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman will be continuing with his cross-examination of you today, and before we proceed, may I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Selak, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll ask the Prosecutor to return to you the statements that you gave to the Prosecution, since we will be referring to them again today. The one I'll be referring to first, sir, is your 1995 statement, the segment that I'm interested in is on page 4 of the English version, a paragraph that begins with, "The Yugoslav Defence forces were comprised of the JNA." Let me know when you've found that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About a third of the way down, the following language appears, "In the late 1980s, the Serb-controlled Yugoslav federal assembly, concerned about TO weapons being in the control of others, passed a law placing the responsibility for the TO weapons storage with the JNA." That's what you said in 1995 and that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at the exhibit, 1572, please. Now, you've seen this document before, last week. The first thing I'd like you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to this document is its date. It's dated the 31 August, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the second thing about that document is - and that's revealed in the body, in the first line - that it is a response to an order from the main staff of the army, seeking an inventory of weapons and equipment issued to TO units and staffs since the beginning of the activities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, the last sentence, General Talic says to the main staff, "Please inform us of your opinion on this matter." Do you have any what that means, what that's about? Why would he be asking for their opinion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Krajina Corps issued weapons and other military equipment to staffs and units of the TO in Croatia and in the Bosnian Krajina. The weapons were registered in the books of the 1st Krajina Corps and the staffs and units of the Territorial Defence did not have their own bookkeeping system so that they were -- there were no records that the weapons had been received and recorded in the subordinated units and staffs to which it had been issued. And for this reason, the corps commander, General Talic, is asking for the opinion of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska as to how to register the weapons and equipment that had been issued to TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes sense now. Now I'd like you to look at the attachment showing the distribution of these weapons. And I want to first of all, if I can, clear up the confusion regarding exactly what the title of that attachment is. As we read it, what it says is - and you correct me if I'm wrong about this - "List of weapons and equipment issued to TO staffs and units from the 5th Corps."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons and equipment that were issued from 5th Corps units to TO staffs and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no indication on this document, is there, about what dates these weapons were issued?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this document. However, as a base commander, I received an identical order to secure logistically all units in Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Kordun, to supply logistically these units. So in addition to the corps, the logistics base too, and I'm talking about 1991, received such an order and that is why I assume that these weapons and equipment were issued in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, one thing we can kind of tell for sure, I think, is due to the fact that a lot of the weapons were issued to TO units located in Croatia, that it occurred during that period of the war in Croatia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the war in Croatia, and also later, because units of the 1st Krajina Corps, that is General Talic's corps, were in Western Slavonia in 1992, an armoured brigade and other units, a part of the rocket brigade was in Glina, close to Karlovac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no indication, is there, on this document or in the cover letter of General Talic as to whether the particular TO units being supplied had been mobilised or not, is there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cannot be seen from this document, but I know for certain that in the Tribunal, there is a document and an order from the general staff of Belgrade and from the command of the 1st and later the 2nd Military District, that the logistics base and the 5th Corps should cover the units in Slavonia, Baranja, and Kordun. The staff from Glina sent me a request for reinforcements of 2.000 men, and in my records, the strength was 500 men, and this document exists in the OTP, and if necessary we can look for it. Even in my notebook, I think this figure can be found. I could try and find it if such proof is required in support of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really think that's not necessary. Let me ask you this: If these were in fact -- it's quite clear, I think that they are -- mobilised TO units, then supplying those units with arms and equipment was perfectly legal and within the guidelines and regulations of the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but with one observation, that the calls for mobilisation went to able-bodied men of Serb ethnicity. I'm talking about Bosnia. A concrete example is that of the municipality of Donji Vakuf. I have the date and statement of the president of the municipality, when he complained that military conscripts of Muslim or Bosniak ethnicity had not received call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you disagree with this, say so, but I think you'll agree that what more often was the case was that Muslims and Croats ignored and refused conscript because they didn't want to get involved in the war in Croatia. That was a major issue at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is true. There were such cases. There were cases of people refusing to be mobilised, but there were also cases when they didn't receive call-up papers because of mistrust as to how they would behave once they were issued weapons in their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, it was suggested, was it not, by Alija Izetbegovic that Bosniaks not respond to these mobilisation calls?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that statement of his. I didn't personally have it in my hands, but I have heard that it exists and I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, looking again at this document, and bearing in mind that there was war going on in Croatia between Croatian military forces and the JNA, let's just look at each one of these entries here. The first, I think, five Okucani and as we go across, are all in Croatia, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next one, Prnjavor was an area located close to Croatia, border region?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the border region between Prnjavor and Croatia there is Bosanska Gradiska but it is nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is it, 30 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That order of magnitude, but I'm not sure, but I think it's around that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Petrinja, that's in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Krupa was at the border, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not quite on the border. It's close, just like Prnjavor but it is not on the border itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omarska isn't either. It's in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Kilometres from the border?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sanski Most about the same?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a little more but about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the same is basically true of the next two. Then we go on over to Bosanska Gradiska. That was on the border?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next three are Banja Luka. The next one is --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 50-odd kilometres from the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next one is Western Slavonia, which is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi which is on the border?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you start looking at the actual weapons and numbers of weapons, what you discover is that the vast majority went to either the border or Croatian units. I don't know if you've done that but we may go through it just briefly here in a minute. If you look at, for instance, automatic rifles, automatic rifles, 7.62 millimetre, the first two columns --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 272 respectively are to Croatia. You go over to --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You go all the way across to Western Slavonia, there is another 581. The large distributions all went to Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding automatic rifles, yes. As for semi-automatic rifles and the others, well, yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at that, you've got the first two columns of the semi-automatic, 980 respectively. There is one large group for Prnjavor. You know that there was a unit from Prnjavor, the wolves of Vucjak, that was actually fighting in the corridor, and that might account for that, might it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to make any comments on that, because the TO units and staffs in the Bosnian Krajina had already received weapons, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. And I would like to ask you to take note of the fact that this report was in -- on the 31st of August, 1992, when combat operations were not so intensive in Croatia then and UN forces were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But this attachment has nothing to do with 1992. This attachment has to do with late 1991 or early 1992, not August, because these TOs in Croatia didn't exist by August, did they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't be 1991. I don't agree. It could only be 1992 because the corps in 1991 would take weapons for its own units that it mobilised in the municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, and it needed weapons. So I know, and I cautioned that there were no records of the weapons issued to the TOs because they didn't return to me certified documents confirming receipt of weapons received from the logistics base in Banja Luka. Therefore, in my view, this document is from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we have another clue as to when it was. We know that it was before 18 May, 1992, don't we, because of its title? It was weapons issued from the 5th Corps, not the 1st Krajina Corps. And the 5th Corps didn't exist after 18 May, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also at the command post of the command of the 5th Corps, which was in the KP Dom in Stara Gradiska in Croatia, there was a discussion with unit commanders of Slavonia. They had received permission for tanks to be delivered to them and I have -- I have in my official notebook the date, how many tanks, how many cannon and how many other weapon should be delivered to staffs in Western Slavonia. Even that some should be pulled out of Knin and taken to warehouses in the KP Dom and elsewhere, and these be under the control of the UN forces, under lock and key. So that the weapons should be under the control of the UN forces but that it should remain the property of SAO Krajina, that is Western Slavonia. And in my official notebook, I have a note of this, the quantities of the equipment that had to be given to Western Slavonia and we don't find here a single tank or APC or other materiel, which General Talic spoke about at the meeting. There should have been T-34 tanks, old models.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's keep going across that column of semi-automatic rifles. You'll see 528 went to Bosanska Gradiska which is on the border; 1491 went to Croatia, Western Slavonia; 535 to other JNA uses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at M-49/57 machine-guns, 50 to Krupa near the border, 150 to Sanski Most. Then in the right-hand column, 150 plus 50 plus 5 plus 4 totals 109. What do you suppose is correct, the total or the individual numbers? Because it's actually 209, if you total.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a mistake in totalling. I think that the number of the weapons that was given to the units is correct. I'm sure the person was in a hurry and it's only human to err.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: M-48 rifles, first two columns, 430 to Croatia, 905 to -- there is 200 there to Croatia; and then 905 to Krupa, which is near the border, 170 other army uses; and finally let's look at zoljas, which are hand-held rocket launchers. If you look at the zoljas, 148, 60, 24 and 60, there in the first columns, all to Croatia, a couple of small numbers, then go all the way over, 160 to Western Slavonia, so virtually all of that is to units in Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The units of the JNA or later the Army of Republika Srpska in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you analyse this document, as to where these weapons were going, the vast majority of them were going either on the border area next to Croatia, where the war was, or in Croatia. And rather than some scheme that got dreamed up by someone that this was an effort to arm civilians in the middle of Republika Srpska, the document basically shows that it was an effort to deal with the war going on in Croatia and arm the units that were fighting there, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it also means that the objective, the purpose, of this was to protect the Serbian people as it was said officially, to protect the Serbian people in the area of the Republic of Croatia and that's the reason why these units remained there. And I repeat, the UN forces controlled these weapons, which had to be stored in warehouses. I don't know what happened later. I never visited the area after that, whether truly the tanks and the guns were in the warehouses or not, I don't know, but I know that they were handed over. You have the document here and the date, but as to the relevant quantities and if -- and whether this went to private homes, I don't think so. That was the TO, the local units. I'm not saying paramilitary units because after all, it was the army that exerted control of these weapons. I mean, if they had issued, handed over the weapons, then they must have had some kind of control over these weapons in order to prevent any abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that they were being issued to Croatia for the purpose of protecting the Serbian people. What other people in the Croatia field of operations were in need of protection?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Croatia field of operations, in the area from Western Slavonia all the way down to Lika, Banija, and other territories further down to Knin, the population was mixed, Croat and Serb, but the majority were Serbs. There were very few Muslims and Bosniaks. The percentage is negligible according to the information that I have, but I think that it can -- this can be easily proved and checked. So once again, it is logical for me that these weapons should have been issued because if we are aware of the military objectives, then we realise that this is only a logical sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is logical, because there are no -- it wouldn't make sense that the JNA would be issuing weapons to protect the Croatian people against whom they are fighting and there are no Muslim people there to protect, and even if they were they would probably be fighting alongside the Croatian fighters. And therefore, the people who they would be issued to protect would logically be the Serbian people. I mean, it just makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at Exhibit P19 now, please. Are you looking at the English version?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you give him the Serbian version, please, the B/C/S version. Now, sir, this is quite a long document and we are only going to speak about the very first few pages. This document speaks of the order we talked about earlier, dealing with the TO weapons having to be turned over to the JNA at one point. Let's just go through some of this. First paragraph, it says, "Pursuant to the order of the head of the chiefs of staff of the armed forces of SFRY, confidential number 19-1, of 14 May, 1990, the action geared to take over and secure the armaments and ammunition of the all people's defence and social self protection subjects in the JNA depots was conducted in the territory of SFRY. The relocation of the TOSR BiH armaments and ammunition was carried out between 18 May and 23 May, 1990, with the exception of the region of Bihac and Banja Luka where it was completed 13 June, 1990. The armed forces took these measures so as to ensure a better and more adequate storage and a safer custody of the armaments and military equipment of the armed forces." Now, that actually happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so by 13 June, 1990, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the TOs had -- the weapons from all of the TO had been taken into custody by the JNA and put into secure storage by the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not put in secure storages in the rear. I mean not all of it. Part of the weapons were taken by the units in those municipalities where brigades and regiments were located. They took those weapons and placed them in their warehouses. I had the same problem for the region of Bihac, Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Banja Luka -- yes, Banja Luka also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just be patient, sir, we are coming to that. If you go over to, I don't know if it's the next page in your document, it's -- there is a small A, the head is the "The Territorial Defence of SR BiH" and the sentence reads, "Until 16 May, 1990, TO of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina kept, stored, the armament and military equipment at 653 locations." Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I haven't found it on page 2, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's probably on page 1 of your document, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then if you go down from there -- so at that point, before the JNA took control of this equipment, it was at 653 different locations. Then if you go down about four paragraphs, you see a paragraph starting with the words, "After the action." And what that says, "After the action, the largest part of the armament and ammunition was amassed at 48 locations." So we went from 653 to 48, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now if we go a little further, we learn that even with that, there were still security problems regarding weaponry and ammunition. For instance, you'll see a paragraph that begins about halfway -- in the English version it's halfway down the page, I don't know where it is in yours. Let me see if I can direct. It's about one, two, three -- it's about four paragraphs after the last one we referred to, beginning with the language, "There have been and still are shortcomings in the custody of armament and ammunition throughout the system as the security comes down to a janitor, a guard, a policeman on duty, and periodical rounds. Only special purpose production enterprises and some larger enterprises have satisfactory security." And then down another couple of paragraphs, there is a section that's headed, "Proposal of measures." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 1, "When the JNA provides the storage conditions, collect all the remaining armament, ammunition, and thereby provide for uniform custody and storage for the TO." Now, that was an effort to even try to do a better job of securing these weapons, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with this, because according to the constitution, the TO was within the competence of the republics. The commands of the bases would send their experts for weapons to the TO warehouses with the purpose of inspecting, storing and protecting weapons in order to prevent any abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, there was a big controversy about that at the time, wasn't there? This was a proposition that was passed by the assembly of the socialist federal Republic of Yugoslavia, SFRY, and two of the republics, Croatia and Slovenia, refused to comply because they said it was an illegal order, illegal law?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true, isn't it? So it was not with without controversy that this happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at number 2, "Gather the information --" well, let me look at the second paragraph of number 1 again. "The commander of the TO of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should adopt a special criterion to regulate the quantity of armament ammunition to be left with the TO headquarters to protect TO plans and facilities." Do you know if this was actually ever carried out, this proposal?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. The objective seems clear to me, that the weapons should be left for the purposes of protection of the TO facilities and staffs. So here specific buildings are in question, so we are talking about the minimum number of weapons for the guards, the janitors and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's really quite set out in the paragraph right before the proposal of measures it says, "Bearing in mind that the TO is a competent part of the armed forces, that the weaponry must be treated in a uniform manner, and that all municipal TOs must keep some of the armaments pistols and riffles, for the protection of persons, documents, flags, plans and TO facilities, there is still a lot of weaponry and ammunition in enterprises and it is -- are -- by and large stored under conditions worse than those that existed in municipal TO depots." And that then would take us down to number 2 under proposal of measures, "Gather the information and views of the enterprises and executive bodies of the sociopolitical communities and by the end of 1990, solve the problem of the armament and ammunition of disbanded war units and enterprises and the surpluses arisen from the reduction of these units. We suggest that these surpluses from the enterprises be turned over free to the TO headquarters." Now I have a couple of things to ask you about that. First of all, what we are talking about here, in addition to sort of normal TO units, within various enterprises, companies, they also had their own in-house TO units and the companies actually had weapons and ammunition stored on the premises for their own internal units, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were work units for the protection of factories and special purposes enterprises. Not every working organisation had this, only special working -- work organisations or enterprises that dealt with some chemicals or lethal substances. So mainly the special purposes enterprises. They were in charge of obtaining such weapons. They bought such weapons themselves. The weapons were under the control of the TO staffs, and the army experts from local bases would, from time to time, carry out adequate checkups of these weapons. The military equipment that was stored in the warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And that's why this says here that, "We suggest that these surpluses from enterprises be turned over free to the TO headquarters." That's a recognition that they had actually been purchased at one point by the enterprise and was owned by them and had not been furnished by the JNA or some other public enterprise. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So all of these TO weapons went from 653 places to 48 places. And when the war in Croatia broke out and TO units were then mobilised and members were called to active service, there was a need to return those weapons to the TO units that they had been taken from in the first place so that they would be properly equipped, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under the condition that an official mobilisation had been publicly declared, a mobilisation of the TO units and staffs. There was an appropriate statutory provision, without a mobilisation having been declared, no units could obtain weapons from the JNA warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And some of the units that actually -- TO units that actually got their weapons returned to them were in areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were majority-Bosniak-Croat areas, true?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this memo and in this list of the weapons that had been returned, it appears that all of the weapons were returned except in the municipality of Hadzici, I think because they had a tank maintenance institute there. I think that only Hadzici retained their weapons. But from this list we can see that all of the weapons mentioned in the report were returned by the 23rd of May. I think that the 13th of June, 1990, was the date that applied in respect of Banja Luka. This order by the general staff was in contravention of the law, of the constitution, and it led to a number of conflicts and disagreements, because weapons were deliberately taken from the republics. The republics which had after all bought all of these weapons and other equipment, which had stored them, which had trained the units, and there were a number of litigations before courts because of this issue, because the assembly of Yugoslavia had taken the prerogatives of the republics. Croatia and Slavonia [sic] did not carry this out, whereas other republics, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro did, Macedonia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and you have hit the heart of the point that I'm trying to make. You're making it better than I am. So we know that within Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA successfully, with rare exception, was able to take control of the TO weapons. But Croatia, for reasons of constitutionality contended that the order was illegal and the TO weapons from the TO units in Croatia were not given into the custody of the JNA, and that's the situation that was in existence when the war broke out between Croatia and the JNA. So you have all of these TO units in Croatia that had never surrendered weapons, TO units in Bosnia-Herzegovina that were unarmed until they could reacquire their weapons. That was the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman, before you move to the next question, just a correction to the transcript, page 20, line 8, we have Croatia and Slavonia, it should be Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may have even said Slavonia. I am totally capable of doing things like that, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after April 7th of 1992, actually arose from a number of TO units that then were formed into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those TO units were able to reacquire their weapons, either legally or illegally, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not aware of such channels in the regions of Gorazde and Sarajevo and how they were armed. I know that there were both legal and illegal channels. I am familiar with the situation in Bosnian Krajina. That was my responsibility and I had part of those weapons. Only the units that had officially declared mobilisation were given these weapons, and legally so. We should not forget that all JNA units that were withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia had to pass through Bosnia and Herzegovina. They left part of their weapons, that is all of it, all of the weapons and the equipment, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As to what channels were used for this purpose, I don't know, but I know that units, some units, took these weapons, unfortunately these weapons were not logged and they remained outside the control of the logistics, logistical bases. I cannot speak about corps. I don't know how they were able to keep this control. However, if we know that the JNA units had over 90 per cent Serbs in their ranks, then we can easily conclude we know where these weapons and this equipment ended. I can show you the documents to this effect for individual municipalities and units, when General Uzelac, for instance, issued an order to issue weapons to the 5th Brigade at Kozara mount - it was a TO brigade that had not been legally, officially mobilised - I had to deal with this problem via Belgrade, because it was illegal. And that's when I clashed with the corps commander, General Uzelac, because of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to look at a document that really maybe tells us a great deal more about this. Would you look, please, at DB126?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, may I please add a few words about this? In the Tribunal, there is a document from the commander of the 6th TO Brigade, Colonel Basara, October 1991. I have a copy of that document, in which he explains emphatically and clearly how he armed the Serb people in Bosnian Krajina, Kljuc, and Sanski Most. So I would like us to look at that document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's interesting, but it has nothing to do with the question I asked you. The question I asked you was about Muslim TO units, and that's what we are going to look at with DB126. This is a document which is written by the person we've talked about before, Mr. Mesud Hasotic, assistant commander for moral guidance and psychological preparation, a colonel and a Bosniak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is it -- it is a document dated 21 April, 1992, which is two weeks after the recognition by the European Community of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at the second paragraph, Colonel Hasotic says this: "Military installations are especially under threat, military industry, depots, and other isolated facilities. Those who are organising the attacks are the republican Territorial Defence staff and the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, while those who carry them out are the SDA and HDZ paramilitary formations." If you go down then to the first numbered paragraph, where he says, "As regards other issues, we wish to mention the following: On the night of 17, 18 April, 1992, the Green Berets and members of the BH MUP special units attacked the Pretis factory in Vogosca and the consequences of these two attacks at 0300 and 0500 hours were the following: Five attackers were killed, 20 wounded, 9 captured, they drove off with seven trucks, two of which contained ammunition. 100 VW Golf vehicles were stolen and the green berets are already using them." Are you familiar with that incident?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us go back to the beginning of this document. Colonel Hasotic simply forwarded this report of the 2nd Military District on the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The report came from the assistant for political and legal affairs of the command of the 2nd Military District, and Colonel Hasotic is not referring to events within the 1st Krajina Corps, that is the 5th Corps area. But he's referring to the whole document and forwarding it to the brigades for their information. This was his professional duty to do. It is not his document but the document of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is the relevance of these areas which are all outside the area that this indictment is concerned with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour what this document does is talk about the acquisition of significant numbers of weapons and materiel by members of Muslim TO units in April of 1992. And as we all know, weapons don't necessarily stay where they are captured but can be transported all over the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's stretching a point. I rather feel this is to show that in other areas, Muslims were receiving arms. We've been through this particular aspect. It is not a defence to say that Muslims were arming themselves. What this case is concerned about is -- the evidence that the Colonel has given relates to the arming, as he alleges, of Serbs within the area that this indictment covers. So, Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning being pursued any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Final comment from you, Mr. Ackerman, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe very strongly that it is -- that it is relevant for us to show that the Muslim, the Bosniak, forces had sources of supply of weapons and could supply those weapons to any place they so chose, including the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are putting the cart before the horse here. I mean, we can't go on like this. As I said, and Ms. Korner said, stretching it too far. You can stretch it as far as you like and build an argument on it. On this corps, you could be asking Colonel and presenting him with documents showing that arms were being bought by Muslims in other countries, on the pretext that they could have then forwarded them to Muslims in the territory of Bosnia Herzegovina. So I think we have to draw a line here, Mr. Ackerman. I think you know exactly what I'm saying, and I would suggest to you to redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think maybe I can -- if I can ask another couple of questions, I can establish more relevance and I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I will stop you if you keep going astray.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was the Pretis factory in Vogosca? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretis in Vogosca or Vogosca municipality is to the west from the center of the city of Sarajevo. It was a component part of the city of Sarajevo. There was a car manufacturing factory there and a special purpose industry, that is military-industrial facilities were there too and it is all within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Military equipment was manufactured there, was it not? Or was it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And another place where military equipment was manufactured in Bosnia-Herzegovina was at the Igman facility near Konjic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to Konjic, some infantry ammunition was being manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the Igman factory?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's Mr. Ackerman's two questions. Where are we now going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I should have to make these representations about where I'm going, but I will. There were only, as I understand it, about two or three factories in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina that manufactured weapons and ammunition. And those factories were all located deep in the interior of the country, in the areas, in the Sarajevo Konjic area for security purposes by Tito when he set up the whole concept of the TO, so that if one is going to try to acquire weapons for use throughout the whole country, by stealing them from these units, these places, then you have to go where they are. I mean, you couldn't go steal weapons in Banja Luka because there wasn't a factory there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we have to stick to the territory that we are talking about. And unless there is at least a prima facie evidence that these weapons ended up in the territory that forms the subject matter of the indictment that we have, I mean, as I said -- I mean, we could have -- we could have instances of weapons being sold and bought by Muslims elsewhere, plus in this case, we have already heard evidence of weapons being sold by Serbs themselves to Muslims. So in actual fact, what is it going to change to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can't put the cart before the horse. I have to go with the horse first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are putting the cart before the horse because you have no evidence at all, at least no indication, at all, even on the prima facie basis, that the weapons allegedly stolen from these two military installations or industries ended up in the hands of the Muslims -- Muslims in the territory that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well let me give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need, Mr. Ackerman, because we have already evidence of Muslims in the territory that we are talking about obtaining weapons from Serb soldiers returning from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, but this is the cart-horse problem. Let's assume I had a witness on the stand who is saying that a great number of weapons were coming into the Bosnian Krajina area from central Bosnia. And then you would say to me: How could that happen? Where did they get the weapons? How can I do that if I don't prove --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you already have this document. This is why Ms. Korner is right in objecting to you pressing forward with the questions, with these questions, with this witness. You have this document which is a document, an official document, by one of the army colonels and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I now -- I object to any further questions on this document. As far as I can see, it is irrelevant to any issue that this officer can help with, and I'd like a ruling so Mr. Ackerman doesn't go on asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you have a ruling, and I object to being restricted on cross-examination. I've made my record and I'm ready to go on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to you look at Exhibit P1573. Now, sir, this is a document that you looked at the other day, so it's not new to you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first question I have with regard to is the date. It's dated 14 March, 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this is at the time where the JNA continued to exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the weapons that are described in this document came from the TO in Banja Luka. That's also true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it indicates that they were transferred with the consent of the TO in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order to transfer it. It hadn't still been transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. It was done with the consent or to be done with the consent of the Banja Luka TO. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: Why is Colonel Tepsic getting involved in what, in effect, involves a transfer of weapons from one TO to another? Why is that any business of his?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vaso Tepsic, assistant commander for logistics, was here abusing his position. He did not have the competence to approve the issuance of ammunition and weapons to TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if this document has any effect at all. I mean, the Banja Luka TO could have simply given those weapons to the Territorial Defence in Karanovac without Tepsic getting involved at all, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But here, we see that arrangements were made between the TO staff of Banja Luka and the corps command. They probably discussed this orally, and Colonel Tepsic on that basis wrote this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us the other day in your testimony, it's page 12.947 of the transcript, that you were not aware of this order of Colonel Tepsic in March of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't aware of this document, and this order has no logic to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told us in the transcript, line 18, "He should have consulted me and there would have been no problem. The district staff of the TO of Banja Luka knew about it but nobody informed me." But I guess what you're saying that it would not have been a problem and there was no problem for these weapons being transferred between these two TO units, just that you didn't know about it?.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it, but if this unit, which was actually a platoon of 30 men, had not been armed, then the municipal TO staff should have requested, through regular channels, such equipment from the logistics base. However, he was asking for them from the corps command, and that is why I'm saying that this was an illegal procedurally, that was not the regular way to supply TO units with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 12948 of your testimony last Wednesday, you were asked this with regard to this document: "It says that he orders that Banja Luka Territorial Defence shall issue the following weapons. So he's giving an order apparently to the Territorial Defence?" Your answer was: "He gave his approval. He approved it." Now, if you look at the document, sir, doesn't it say, "I hereby order"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says, "I hereby order."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's not an approval, it's an order, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you say that it was an approval? Why did you say that he didn't order it, he approved it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a slip I made. The document is quite specific. It says, "I order." He won't be issuing the weapons but the operator who was where the weapons were stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you find it strange that a JNA officer would order a TO unit to do what it was they wanted to do anyhow? Why was that necessary? Why would he have to order them to do it? I think I've asked that and it's been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's more, Your Honour, what Mr. Ackerman hasn't actually pointed out to the witness is the furthers explanation he gave as to why Colonel Tepsic should be giving this order or approval which follows directly on in the LiveNote he's quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go on now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at DB116, and at the same time, you can also be given DB117. Now, DB116, sir, is another similar order signed by Tepsic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one is dated 5 May, 1992, still the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one says, "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the 5th Corps, at the briefing on 4 May and with the goal of supplying units and Territorial Defence staffs with weapons and raising their level of combat readiness, I hereby order military post 79, 80, Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What happened what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard a strange voice that mentioned Mr. Brdjanin's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's important that the witness is hearing the interpretation, because I could follow your question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems that there may be a problem, I'm not quite sure that there is one. Colonel, have you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters had some problem with the equipment. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You have heard -- have had Mr. Ackerman's question translated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had heard of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the number was mentioned and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what military post 7980 in Banja Luka was.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a subordinated unit, subordinated to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it is --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit this was, but every brigade had its military post. So the number of the military post is the secret name or the confidential name for the unit. It's not really secret. It was used in -- under peacetime conditions. In wartime, different numbers were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this was a brigade, basically, military post, 7980?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. Someone from one of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, were you there in Banja Luka. Were you familiar with military post 7980?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is familiar. I've forgotten the location, and I wouldn't like to make an error. I'm not sure. So if you have the information yourself, I will think it over. The number does ring a bell. It is Banja Luka. I'm not sure which military post this was. There were very many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's rather difficult to keep all that in one's mind. There were military posts in the subordinate units of the base, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at the signature and more importantly the stamp that's on this document. The signature and so forth, of course, is assistant commander for logistics, Colonel Vaso Tepsic. But the stamp there says, "Military post 4022, Banja Luka." Can you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Ackerman, are you finished with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to 117 next, Your Honour, so I'm finished with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, just a simple question: You see in document DB116, we have got two localities mentioned, two TOs, basically, one of Bosanska Gradiska and the other one of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in each case, we have 50 pieces of automatic rifles, 7.62, 150 pieces of semi-automatic rifles. If you go back to the document, P1572, that you were questioned upon earlier, you'll see that -- do you still have that document, 1572? So please, that's the document which had the list --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar? Could you please give the witness -- now, if you look at this document, 1572, which you had seen before, under the column Bosanska Gradiska, you will see that there are only 30 automatic rifles, although there are 528 semi-automatic rifles. And you will also see that Kotor Varos does not appear in the list shown on P1572. Could that possibly mean that the list contained in Exhibit P1572 refers to a period in time prior to the 5th of May, 1992, which is the date of Exhibit DB116?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite obvious that weapons were being duplicated here. This was a unit consisting of 200 men in both municipal staffs, and it did not -- it was not covered in this list dated the 31st of August on the weapons issued. However, the corps command and its units would obtain supplies for all units subordinated to them, even without orders, all units that were carrying out their orders. As I was saying, even paramilitary units, because I have a document, and I saw it here in the Tribunal, which reports clearly the number of paramilitary formations within the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So clearly, Colonel Tepsic, without consulting General Talic, I believe, issued, on his own initiative, this order. He had the authority to do that. He was the competent person. And the document is quite legal. But I do underline that Bosanska Gradiska, for Bosanska Gradiska, in the TO staff, there were only Serb soldiers, that is those units consisted exclusively of Serbs. As for Kotor Varos, I believe the situation was similar but I cannot guarantee, I'm not 100 per cent sure, as I am for Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a 15-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, we are still talking about this document, DB116 and in answer to the Judge's question, you said this: "So clearly, Colonel Tepsic, without consulting General Talic, I believe, issued, on his own initiative, this order." That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, but I must apologise. In the introduction it says, "Pursuant to an oral order issued by the corps commander." It was my mistake. Colonel Tepsic did receive an order of the 5th Corps commander to issue these weapons. My apologies once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what information it was that you have that caused to you conclude that this order was issued without consulting General Talic? Or did you just make that up?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't just make it up, because Colonel Tepsic brought me, as the commander of the base, an automatic rifle. It was a gift from him, and I know that he gave same gifts to other officers. There was a bed in his office under which there was a box of automatic rifles. I asked him, "What do you keep these for?" And he just smiled. In my notebook, I have the number of the rifle that he gave me, and my Chief of Staff, Colonel Cengic. I have the number of this rifle in my notebook, the official number, which means that he issued, and he gave the similar weapons to other people, and it was quite shocking for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can move forward, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you before I go on to the next document, I just want to ask you a couple of general questions, so that we kind of understand the general situation. TO units were not under the command of the 5th Krajina Corps? TO units located in the area of responsibility of the 5th Krajina Corps were not under the command of the 5th Krajina Corps, were they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, that there was a regional staff of the TO headquartered in Banja Luka, that existed a long time before the Autonomous Region of Krajina was ever created?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief was Colonel Nikola Kasabascic the Chief of Staff of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of the regional TO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, interpreter's correction, commander of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It used to be referred to as the zone TO, whose commander was a Colonel Nikola Kasabasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how about Colonel Milorad Sajic, what role did he play with regard to that regional TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. It is possible that he was the Chief of Staff, but the exact function during that period of time, I don't know. I'm not sure, because the situation changed within six months. A large number of officers came from Slovenia and Croatia, who took up functions, offices, that had been previously held by those Croats and Muslims who had left the JNA. So I don't know during which period of time who had which particular function. I'm familiar only with the key officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one last question with regard to this document, DB116, and that is: Were you familiar with it at the time, in May of 1992? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the existence of this document, no. I saw it here in the courtroom for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look now at DB117. This is a similar kind of document, signed by Colonel Tepsic, dated 9 May, 1992, still JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was four days after the last one we just looked at, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this orders military post 7980, Banja Luka, to deliver additional materiel to Kotor Varos TO, does it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, the English translation that we have says military post office box 4022 and military post office box 7980, that's not an accurate translation, is it? It's military post, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, this one says it's pursuant to a verbal order by the 5th Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 4022 is the number of the corps command. That's the peacetime number of this military post, because in correspondence between units and civilian structures, usually the number of the military post would be mentioned, and not the name of the formation, the brigade, the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And again, were you aware of this order in May of 1992 when it was entered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see this document for the first time. But it was on the basis of an oral order of the corps command that Tepsic ordered issuance of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've now seen three similar orders signed by Tepsic which you told us you did not see before. You were aware, weren't you, that Tepsic was doing this, that he was signing orders of this kind?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for logistics, and this concerns the logistical tasks and Colonel Tepsic was in charge of that. He acted on the basis of the orders issued by his commander, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but you haven't answered my question. You were aware, weren't you, that Tepsic was doing this, that he was signing orders of this kind at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of a logistical base and Colonel Tepsic was with the corps command. He was the assistant commander for logistics and we never discussed, nor was he under any obligation to inform me about the existence of these documents. This was an order that he issued to his subordinate units, and there was no need whatsoever for him to inform me thereof, nor was I interested in that. If he had contacted me, then I would have probably initialed the document in the upper right corner and sent this to the chief of technical services to deal with this problem. The corps had weapons, and Colonel Tepsic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Were you aware that he was doing this or not? I think your answer is no, you were not aware, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he had written this. I didn't know that he had regulated this in a document. I can see the initial of the person who processed this document, DJ. This person was probably in charge of weapons. The official who was in charge of the weapons. So he was probably the one who typed out this document and he signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to insist, sir, that you answer my question. The question is very simple: You were aware, weren't you, that Tepsic was doing this, that he was signing orders of this kind? Were you aware or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not. I didn't know that he wrote this type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman. Try, Colonel, I know that you are doing this in a sense of cooperation with this Tribunal, but on the other hand, please try to be concise in your answers and answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. Don't go beyond what Mr. Ackerman is asking you because that way, we will never finish. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have in front of you, sir, your statement from 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. It's been returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know where it went.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The part I'm interested in is it's page 10 in the English version. It's a paragraph that begins with, "Colonel General Nikola Uzelac, the commander of the Banja Luka Corps in 1991. He received two promotions during the war." Tell me when you find that. Page 11, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want you to go down one, two, three paragraphs from that, and you'll see a paragraph which reads as follows: "During late 1991 and 1992, Uzelac's assistant to the commander for logistics Colonel Vaso Tepsic would come to me regularly at the end of the day with orders for weapons for new brigades being formed in the local TOs." You did know about this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We held regular, daily meetings, at which the logistical supplies of the corps were analysed. There were also meetings, both his and mine, with chiefs of relevant departments, and all the issues concerning logistical supply of the corps were discussed during those meetings, including these units mentioned here. But without documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said was that he came to you regularly at the end of the day with orders, like these orders we've been looking at. He came to you with orders for new brigades being formed in the local TOs. These orders were for the distribution of weapons to TOs. And you're talking here about him bringing those orders to supply those new brigades being formed in the TOs and that's what you told the Prosecutor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the word "order" is being used in the context you are suggesting, Mr. Ackerman, and not in some other context, because an order for weapons means one thing, an order issued by Colonel -- by Colonel Tepsic to the post 7980, to supply, furnish, so many weapons to a TO is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How could that be? An order is an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, if the TO in Kotor Varos places an order for 100 rifles --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an order too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I want to make sure that what is shown as with orders for weapons for new brigades is what you meant and not what I am suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like me to ask him that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The solution lies in the original language, which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the statement was taken in English and then translated into -- so it's not the original language used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But perhaps the witness can enlighten us. I don't know what's written in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, it's not what the witness said in Serbo-Croat was written down. The witness -- we went through it, it's a long time ago. You may remember, statements are taken in English so it's witness answer, interpreter's translation, and then that's written down, and then read back, maybe by the same interpreter, maybe not. And what's happened is the whole statement has been translated since it was decided that he would be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put a direct question to the witness myself, Mr. Ackerman. Here it says, "During late 1991 and 1992, Colonel Tepsic would come to me regularly at the end of the day with orders for weapons for new brigades being formed." What do you mean by "orders for weapons"? In other words, was Colonel Tepsic coming to you and telling you, "Colonel Selak, we need so many rifles for the TO in Kotor Varos or the TO in Bosanska Gradiska"? Or was he coming to you with an order ready only to be signed or confirmed by you for the supply of weapons to the various Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. TOs? Because the way it's written here, in my opinion, leaves a little bit of a question mark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to give you a larger explanation. We had regular meetings, Colonel Tepsic and myself, with our assistants, the chiefs of departments. Colonel Tepsic never issued an order for weapons. It was his official in charge of technical services, in charge of weapons, who would tell us about the situation, and then Tepsic would submit a request for the replenishment of these units, not in writing. It would be discussed on the following day and then a request for appropriate documents would be made. That's why I see this document here for the first time, and there was no need for such a document to reach me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that's clear enough, Mr. Ackerman. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We are going to go to a completely different subject now, sir. I'm finished with that and with those documents. I want to you look now -- I think you turn back one page in your statement of 1995. You should find a paragraph that begins with the language, "With respect to the issue of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What that says is, "With respect to the issue of responsibility of senior commanders for the actions of their subordinates in the field, there is no way that a commander in the field would commit a unit to combat without the permission of his commander." And you said something very similar to that in your testimony here, I think, Wednesday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there such a concept in the JNA that in the U.S. army we call rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were combat rules pertaining to the use of units, and the authority in terms of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are -- there were regulations regarding what a unit could do under certain prescribed situations, and I'll get specific here in a minute, but that was well set out in the regulations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, please, what those rules are if a military unit is attacked? If the unit is attacked, surely they don't have to wait for permission from the commander before they can engage?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commander immediately undertakes a defence. At the same time, he is supposed to inform his superior commander that he has been attacked, and that fighting is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what are his standing orders at that point, beyond informing his commander, what is he required to do? What is he supposed to do pursuant to regulations at that point, when his unit is attacked?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He will use his unit to carry out the task, to defend his unit, the ground, the terrain, and to report his superior commander whether he may need assistance, or the degree to which the task has been carried out. So he must regularly inform his superior in a successive way so that the superior should be well informed on what was happening on the battle front and what he needed to do to send him support and other things, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if possible, and to the extent possible, he is to totally eliminate the threat to his unit, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why the unit exists. That is why it has been formed to carry out the task assigned to by its commander. The commander has already taken the decision to engage the unit in that part of the theatre, and he is acting on that decision. He had to assess himself who the enemy was, how strong the enemy was, and what the aims of the enemy were in order to be able to take adequate countermeasures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And what I said to you and asked you, I think you could have said is true. If possible and to the extent possible, he is to totally eliminate the threat to his unit, isn't he? That's true?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to now look at your statement from the year 2000. The English version, sir, we are going to page 5, talking about brigades and authorities, things of that nature. And the paragraph I'm directing your attention to reads as follows: "I am not aware of any brigade operations."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I haven't found the passage yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's on page 5, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 5, second paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
